proposals.relationship: Iacovetta identifies Thompson’s Making of the English Working Class as the foremost inspiration for her thesis and first book’s treatment of class as lived experience.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1999:277 explicitly names this inspiration and develops class identity through everyday material lives, culture and protest. She also names Taylor/Ross feminist correctives to its artisan/skilled-male emphasis and retains a Thompsonian sensibility in her own work. Original Thompson book and1992monograph unread; her retrospective testimony, not a claim of formal supervision or wholesale agreement.
primary_locators: Iacovetta1999:277/main paragraph and nn5–6; saved primary indexed277witness

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta names Hobsbawm among the British Marxist historians highly influential in the intellectual formation of her thesis and first book.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1999:277 places Hobsbawm alongside Samuel and a wider North American labour/feminist/immigration constellation, beneath the particularly specified Thompson inspiration. No particular Hobsbawm book, exclusive lineage, direct teaching or full agreement inferred from this explicit bounded formation testimony.
primary_locators: Iacovetta1999:277,paragraph beginning Like much new social and labour history

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta identifies Gregory Kealey among the North American historians highly influential in shaping her thesis and first book.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1999:277 names Gregory Kealey in the formative scholarly constellation.1997:23 additionally credits Greg Kealey’s input and re-use permission, distinct roles that do not by themselves establish formation. Gregory S.Kealey is not Linda Kealey, her1996coauthor. Original Kealey studies unread; no automatic formal supervisory role.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta credits Sangster among feminist labour historians whose work helped her develop a class, gender and race/ethnicity framework.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1999:278 explicitly situates her paradigm in debates among labour, ethnic and feminist historians and names Sangster among North American feminists writing immigrant/ethnic women workers and gender politics. This positive formation resource differs from preserved mutual1996critique1614/1615 and retains Linda Kealey coauthorship of that exchange. Specific Sangster monograph/edition not identified here; no full original reading.
primary_locators: Iacovetta1999:278,paragraphs on class-gender-race/ethnicity paradigm and North American feminist labour history

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta uses Higham’s long-range study of nativism as a benchmark for what Canadian immigration historiography had yet to produce.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1997:4 identifies Strangers in the Land’s broad chronology and shifting targets/commonalities, then distinguishes narrower Canadian group studies and Howard Palmer’s Alberta exception. This is a specific historiographical benchmark, not evidence of personal mentorship or wholesale adoption; Howard Palmer is not Bryan D.Palmer. Higham/Palmer originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta presents Parr’s analysis of masculinity, skill and Germanness as a model for connecting gender with ethnicity in immigrant labour history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1997:12 invokes Gender of Breadwinners while arguing that earlier manliness studies insufficiently linked masculinity and ethnicity;4 separately praises Labouring Children as gender-conscious analysis. Bounded analytical resource for her historiographical argument, not every Parr thesis or original monograph checked. Existing group958/1170 routes are not already a Parr→Iacovetta personal resource.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta uses Gordon’s family-violence and welfare history to analyze gendered, racialized and class-based institutional encounters and mediated case files.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1997:15 explicitly takes Gordon as a productive example of public/private and welfare encounters;2019:36/44 cites Heroes and the Scott–Gordon exchange for risks of misreading caseworker paradigms and subjective judgments. The exchange does not imply identical Scott/Gordon positions.1997bibliography34prints Heroes1980 whereas2019prints1989Penguin; neither printed date is silently treated as first-edition verification. Originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta uses the Scott–Gordon exchange as a methodological resource for interpreting mediated social-work case files.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2019:36 cites the1990exchange alongside Gordon and Peel when warning that ignorance of caseworkers’ paradigms and professional/subjective judgments produces misinterpretation. This records the exchange as a resource involving Scott, not proof agreement with every Scott position or original formation of Iacovetta’s1992book;1999:276 explicitly distinguishes gendered approaches developed outside Scott/poststructuralism. Scott and Gordon are interlocutors, not assumed coauthors of a single shared argument; original exchange unread.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta uses McKay’s antimodernism analysis to frame ethnic spectacle while emphasizing its modern nation-building purpose.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2019:30 gives historical festival context and35 explicitly cites McKay1994 together with Hoganson2007 for liberal anti-modernism, then qualifies the nostalgia as serving new modernity and nation-building. This particular conceptual application is not automatic agreement with all Quest of the Folk interpretations or sole credit for a multi-source frame; originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta adapts Pratt’s contact-zone concept to unequal interactions between immigrant counsellors and clients.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2019:35–36/n11 explicitly places the Institute in a contact zone with asymmetrical power and cites Imperial Eyes1992. She also retains entangled narratives, partial negotiations and variable outcomes. Bounded methodological resource, not direct reading proof for every chapter or a universal account of all migration; Pratt original unread.

proposals.relationship: Iacovetta draws on Foucault to frame social workers’ power in local encounters while stressing that they did not exercise full control.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2019:36/n12 explicitly attaches the Foucault reference to this local-power claim and immediately distinguishes varied outcomes. Cited title printed Knowledge/Power(London1980); actual collection/translation/editorial apparatus unread, not certified as a sole-authored French original. Basok/Bastable213criticize underdeveloped theoretical allusions in earlier Gatekeepers, a distinct work/time; this narrow later use does not refute their assessment or prove broad Foucauldian formation.
